text.text: A ten-minute tour of the building in this workspace. Share it with receiving, shipping, inventory control and the warehouse manager.
: each SKU with its brand, location, zone, velocity class, units per case, units on hand and available to promise.
: what is coming in, with PO or ASN number, pallets, units expected and received, and condition.
: the schedule for every door, inbound and outbound.
: what is going out, by channel, with ship-by date and tracking.
: each pick task by wave, picked in full or short.
: what was counted, the variance and the reason.
7 am: release today's orders as picks; check the dock schedule.
Morning: receiving at the doors; morning wave picked and packed.
Afternoon: putaway; afternoon wave; freight pickups.
End of day: everything due shipped or on hold, staging lanes empty.
Every morning: dock appointments, picks due, counts scheduled
Every day: damage and shortages reported to brands
Every week: cycle counts scheduled by velocity class
Every month: count accuracy and short picks reviewed

The receiving lead owns the dock and putaway. The shipping lead owns waves, packing and carriers. The inventory controller owns counts and adjustments. The warehouse manager reads accuracy, on-time shipping and the dock schedule.
No stock moves without a location. No adjustment without a recount. No carrier at a door without an appointment. Damage is photographed before anything else happens.

text.text: Receiving is where inventory accuracy is won or lost. A mistake at the dock follows the stock through every pick and count after it. This is the procedure every receiver follows, every truck.

The moisturizer restock arrived at Door 1 with one crushed pallet. The receiver photographed it, counted 3,540 good units against 3,600 expected, marked the condition as Some damage and emailed the brand before lunch. The good units went to the pick face, which was nearly empty.
Orders leave on time when picks are released early, picked in waves and checked before they are sealed. This is the shipping day, from release to the trailer door.

A short pick means the system said the stock was there and it was not. Every one triggers a cycle count of that location within two days.

The spa retail moisturizer order was released in the morning wave, but the pick face held only 50 units and reserve was empty. The picker marked it short, the order went on hold and the brand was told. A count was booked for the next day, and the morning delivery at Door 1 refilled the location.
Counting a few locations every day beats shutting the building for a yearly stocktake. Cycle counts keep the numbers right, and the reasons behind each difference tell you which process to fix.
Also count straight away after a short pick, a damaged delivery or a brand's query.

The pet bed count found 418 against 420 expected. A second counter agreed. The last two outbound picks showed one order picked with an extra bed, so the reason was Mis-pick and the brand's customer was contacted. The location label had faded, and was replaced the same day.
